JSON: Name: hypergraph_mamba_nodeclf Title: Hypergraph neural network with a Mamba-inspired state-space fusion for improved node classification Short Hypothesis: Fusing adjacency-based and role-based node embeddings via a Mamba-inspired state-space fusion before hypergraph convolution and using residual connections yields at least a 2.0 percentage-point absolute increase in Micro-F1 for node classification compared with the best adjacency-only GNN baseline on standard benchmark datasets. Related Work: Existing approaches for node classification either aggregate local adjacency information via message-passing GNNs (e.g., spectral and spatial convolutions, graph attention) or learn role/structural embeddings via unsupervised methods (random-walk embeddings, structural diffusion/wavelet methods). Graph transformer variants and pretrained graph models capture long-range context but incur quadratic attention cost and limited structural inductive bias. Hypergraph neural methods model higher-order relationships but typically rely on a single hypergraph construction strategy and do not jointly fuse explicit role representations with adjacency features; they also can overfit to unsupervised role features or suffer over-smoothing in deep stacks. State-space sequence models provide linear-time long-range modeling but have not been widely integrated into graph representation pipelines. Limitations across prior work therefore include: reliance on adjacency-only aggregation, unsupervised role features that do not transfer well to supervised tasks, quadratic attention cost for global modeling, single-strategy hypergraph construction, and sensitivity to over-smoothing when stacking layers. Abstract: We address the gap between adjacency-driven graph neural networks and explicit role-aware node representations by proposing a unified framework that fuses role-based and adjacency-based embeddings via a Mamba-inspired structured state-space mechanism and propagates the fused representation through hypergraph convolutional layers with residual connections. The method constructs two complementary hypergraphs—one from local node-link neighborhoods and one from global node-degree groups—to capture higher-order adjacency and role similarity. A learnable state-space fusion adaptively weights and compresses the two embedding streams in linear time, enabling long-range dependency modeling without quadratic attention. The fused embeddings are processed by hypergraph convolutions to jointly learn higher-order interactions while residual paths mitigate over-smoothing. The main contribution is the integration of dual hypergraph construction with a trainable state-space fusion module in a single supervised node-classification model. We expect the approach to produce more discriminative node embeddings and consistent gains in Micro-F1 and robustness across diverse benchmark datasets compared with adjacency-only and existing hypergraph baselines. Experiments: Datasets: use Cora, Citeseer, Pubmed, ACM, DBLP, IIP, TerroristRel, ENZYMES subsets (E118,E123,E295,E296,E297), ogbn-arxiv, and ogbn-products. Data splits: stratified 70/15/15 train/validation/test; report mean±std over 5 independent seeds (10 seeds for smaller ENZYMES splits, 50 seeds for very small datasets where applicable). Baselines: GCN, GAT, GraphSAGE, JumpingKnowledge GNN, StrucGCN/Struc2vec, DeepWalk, Node2vec, hypergraph convolutional network (single hypergraph variants), HGCN(adjacency only), Graphormer, GPS, SAN, GROVER, GraphMAE. Evaluation metrics: Micro-F1 (primary), Accuracy, macro-F1, AUC for multi-class where applicable, training time per epoch (s), peak GPU memory (GB), and explanation fidelity/sparsity for interpretability evaluation. Implementation & hyperparameters: two hypergraph convolution layers unless otherwise specified, dropout 0.5, Adam optimizer lr=0.003, weight decay=5e-4, hidden dims ∈ {60,80,100,120,140} (report sensitivity), early stopping on validation for max 200 epochs. Statistical test: paired t-test (α=0.05) comparing proposed method vs best baseline per dataset. Ablation studies: (A) remove Mamba block (replace with simple linear attention/fusion), (B) remove residual connection, (C) degree-only hypergraph, (D) neighborhood-only hypergraph, (E) raw features only vs pretrained Node2vec+GraphWave inputs, (F) vary hypergraph-conv depth from 1 to 8, (G) vary hidden dim. Additional comparisons: compute/efficiency ablation comparing state-space fusion vs full attention (quadratic) in time and peak memory on ogbn-arxiv and ogbn-products. Interpretability: use HGExplainer and adapted GraphLIME to quantify fidelity and sparsity on ACM and DBLP for 10 validation nodes; report average fidelity and sparsity. Success criteria: proposed model must show ≥2.0 absolute Micro-F1 improvement over best adjacency-only baseline on at least 4 of the medium/large datasets and statistically significant (p<0.05) aggregate improvement across all datasets. Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Hypergraph construction sensitivity: degree-based and neighborhood-based hypergraphs may not capture relevant role-similarity on all domains; fixed construction rules can introduce spurious ties. 2) Dependency on pretrained role embeddings: downstream gains may rely on quality of external role embeddings (GraphWave, Node2vec); poor embeddings reduce benefit. 3) Over-smoothing and depth sensitivity: despite residuals, deep hypergraph convolution stacks may still produce indistinguishable node representations on some graphs. 4) State-space limitations: Mamba-inspired SSMs assume a particular linear state structure and can fail to adaptively compress highly input-dependent interactions in certain graphs. 5) Scalability: while state-space fusion is linear-time, large hyperedge counts or very dense incidence matrices increase memory and runtime; constructing hypergraphs for million-node graphs may be infeasible. 6) Evaluation biases: node-class distributions and stratified splits can hide real-world class imbalance or temporal covariate shift; benchmark improvements may not generalize to evolving or heterogeneous graphs. 7) Interpretability limits: post-hoc explainers for heterogeneous hypergraphs are approximate and may misattribute importance across metapaths. 8) Computational resource requirements: training with dual hypergraphs and SSM blocks requires nontrivial GPU memory and tuning, limiting reproducibility for low-resource settings.
